memory_verse.label: Bible Reference
memory_verse.text: "and I have filled him with the Spirit of God, with wisdom, with understanding, with knowledge and with all kinds of skills — to make artistic designs for work in gold, silver and bronze, to cut and set stones, to work in wood, and to engage in all kinds of crafts." - Exodus 31:3-5 (NIV)

devotion.label: Devotion
devotion.text:
This is the first time in Scripture that anyone is described as filled with the Spirit of God — and it is a craftsman. Not a prophet, not a priest, not a king. A man who works with gold, stone, and wood. God fills him with the Spirit specifically so he can design and build beautifully.

That should reshape how we think about spiritual gifting. We tend to divide life into sacred work and secular work, assuming God is interested in preaching and prayer but indifferent to carpentry and metalwork. Exodus 31 says otherwise. Bezalel's ability to cut a stone well was Spirit-given, and God took credit for it.

Whatever you do with your hands or mind — building, cooking, teaching, repairing, designing, farming, keeping accounts — the skill itself came from God. Paul writes that there are different kinds of gifts, but the same Spirit distributes them all (1 Cor 12:4-6). Your competence is not separate from your discipleship. Do your work well, and know that the ability to do it well was itself a gift. God is honoured by good craftsmanship, whatever the craft.

reflection.label: Reflection
reflection.text:
Do I see my practical skills as Spirit-given, or as unrelated to my faith?
How would I approach my work differently if I saw my ability as God's gift?

prayer.label: Prayer
prayer.text: Father, You gave me the skills I have and You are honoured when I use them well. Help me see no division between my work and my worship, and do everything for You. Amen.
